common_name: Shells Of Dallas Daylily (Parent of Alyne Fisher)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Shells Of Dallas is a Hemerocallis cultivar documented chiefly as one of the two parents, crossed with Little Infant, behind Ury Winniford's 1982 introduction Alyne Fisher. No detailed record of its own flower color, form, or registration year survives in the sources consulted, a common gap for breeding-line parent cultivars whose only lasting record is a cross formula behind a better-documented offspring. Grow it, as with other Texas-bred daylily lines of its era, in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to sustain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Region 6 — Histories of Daylily Names

common_name: False River Louisiana Iris (Parent of Faubourg-Saint John)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: False River is a Louisiana iris documented as one of the two parents, crossed with Helen Naish, behind New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor's 2001 introduction Faubourg-Saint John, which O'Connor later self-crossed to produce the award-winning German Coast. No detailed record of False River's own flower color or registration survives in the sources consulted, likely named for the oxbow lake of the same name along the Mississippi River in Louisiana's Pointe Coupee Parish. Grow it, as with other Louisiana iris hybrids, in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)
